perf(mcp): keep Playwright and type-only imports off MCP startup (#1691)

* fix(build): emit no runtime imports for type-only bindings

Under verbatimModuleSyntax, an import whose specifiers all carry inline
`type` modifiers compiles to `import {} from "..."`, a side-effect import
that still resolves and evaluates the module. 78 compiled modules carried
one, including `import {} from "playwright-core"` in the browser scenario
session, which loaded Playwright's module graph at MCP startup.

Use top-level `import type` for these bindings and enable oxlint's
typescript/no-import-type-side-effects rule so the pattern cannot return.

Refs #1685

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* perf(mcp): load Playwright when a scenario launches, not at startup

The browser scenario and Electron active providers are constructed before
the stdio server serves, and both bound Playwright's launchers at module
load. Resolve `chromium` and `_electron` from playwright-core when a
capture opens instead, as the web module resolver already does.

MCP startup now resolves 1,312 modules (4,902 resolutions) instead of
1,598 (6,076) before reading the first request, and no longer loads
playwright-core. Provider construction, the tool catalog, and capability
inventory are unchanged.

A boundary test spawns the stdio server, initializes, lists tools, and
asserts playwright-core and isomorphic-git were not resolved; the CLI
probe now exercises the real launch path to prove detection.

feat(update): update Bun global installations (#1735)

* feat(update): update Bun global installations

`rea update` only recognized npm global installations and looked up
releases with `npm view`, so a `bun add --global rea-agents` install on a
machine without npm failed with `spawn npm ENOENT`.

Detect the running package inside Bun's global directory
(BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_DIR, $BUN_INSTALL/install/global,
$XDG_CACHE_HOME/.bun/install/global, ~/.bun/install/global), resolve the
latest release with `bun info`, install with
`bun add --global --ignore-scripts`, then verify the installed entry point
and plan integration maintenance exactly as for npm.

Bun commands run inside the owning global directory with
BUN_INSTALL_GLOBAL_DIR pinned, so the caller's current project is never
selected. A global directory without package.json is not treated as an
owned installation: Bun then installs into the nearest ancestor project.
npm installations keep their existing commands and messages.

* fix(update): gate Bun self-updates on supported CLI versions

commits.body:
fix(bun): report the real runtime and enforce worker memory budgets on Windows (#1730)

* fix(bun): report the real runtime and enforce worker memory budgets on Windows

Under Bun, REA recorded Node/V8 identity it did not observe and its JavaScript helper processes ran without a memory bound, because Bun ignores the V8 heap flags REA passes. Source-map trace Evidence claimed runtime node-v8 with Bun's synthetic V8 heap limit (the decoder then rejected that limit, so trace_web_source_location always failed), analysis resource failures reported heap limits Bun does not enforce, the HAR decoder claimed a fixed 192 MiB heap, and doctor reported Bun's Node.js compatibility version as the Node version.

Identify the runtime once from process.versions. Source-map reports record id bun with the Bun and Node.js compatibility versions and a null v8_heap_limit_bytes; the decoder checks the heap budget only for V8 reports and rejects a report from a runtime other than the launching one. The analysis worker reports a null heap limit under Bun, HAR limitations and failures omit heap sizes under Bun, and the doctor node check reports Bun and passes when its Node.js compatibility version is supported.

On Windows under Bun, each helper's owned Job Object now carries a commit limit of its heap budget plus a measured 512 MiB Bun runtime reserve (704 MiB for the codec and HAR decoder, 1536 MiB for the default analyzer). The native addon accepts an optional page-aligned job memory limit on process_spawn, verifies it by readback, associates a private completion port before the child is created, and reports a sticky memoryLimitReached and peak job commit on each poll; inspect reports jobMemoryLimit. A requested limit with an artifact lacking the control refuses the launch, and non-Windows launchers refuse a limit.

Reaching the limit is classified by the job notification rather than Bun's exit status: the analyzer fails the current source with a memory resource failure reporting worker_process_memory_limit_bytes, the codec returns a memory resource failure, and the HAR decoder returns its memory failure with process_memory_limit_bytes. Bun source-map Evidence records process_memory_limit_bytes, verified against the launcher. Node.js launches and outputs are unchanged.

* fix(windows): drain memory notifications after observing exit

* fix(managed): charge retained member facts instead of decoding bounds

inspect_managed_members returned no types or methods for ordinary
assemblies: Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.3 (netstandard2.0, 705 KB) exceeded
the 64 MiB representation budget. Each method body reserved 256 bytes
per IL byte and each signature 256 bytes per blob byte before decoding,
and those worst-case bounds were never returned, so the budget scaled
with total IL size rather than with the retained output. The final
projection admission also charged every decoded string at six bytes per
character and every scalar at 32 bytes, about eight times its JSON size.

Bound IL, exception-clause and signature decoding with a transient
admission that does not consume capacity, then reserve the decoded body
or signature that is actually retained. Projection admission now
charges the exact UTF-8 JSON bytes of decoded strings, keys and scalars;
escaped and multibyte text still counts at its encoded size.

Newtonsoft.Json now yields 496 types, 4185 methods and 18846 call
edges. Assemblies whose retained facts exceed the budget, such as the
2.3 MB System.Private.ServiceModel 4.7.0, remain unavailable.

* fix(managed): bound concurrent decoding and count JSON bytes in place

Review follow-up. A method's IL bound and its exception-section bounds
were each checked against the same remaining capacity although their
bookkeeping is live at the same time, so 40 MiB of IL plus 40 MiB of
exception clauses passed a 64 MiB budget. Transient admissions now
accumulate until the method body or signature is built, and reserve
respects bounds that are still live.

Projection admission also serialized each decoded string to measure it,
which could allocate about six times a near-limit string before the
check. It now counts the exact escaped UTF-8 bytes without building the
JSON text.

* fix(managed): admit derived call and field edges as they are built

Review follow-up. Released IL bounds no longer stand in for the call and field-access records that edges() derives from anchors. Each record is now admitted before the graph grows further, so a crafted assembly cannot materialize the whole derived graph before the representation guard fails.

commits.subject: fix(install): describe automatic setup and guard truncated downloads (#1902)
commits.body:
fix(install): describe automatic setup and guard truncated downloads (#1902)

* fix(install): describe automatic setup and guard truncated downloads

The help text said the installer only installs the CLI and that
`rea setup` must be run separately, but the installer starts
`rea setup` interactively whenever a terminal is available. Describe
that behaviour and the --no-setup/--no-prompt opt-out.

Wrap the installer body in `main` and call it on the last line, so a
truncated `curl | bash` download fails to parse instead of executing a
partial script. Behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

Add an installer scenario that runs a copy truncated right after the
npm install line and requires that it prints nothing and never invokes
npm; it fails against the previous script.

Validation: bash -n, shellcheck 0.10.0, installScript boundary tests.

* fix(install): require the closing token before running main

Wrapping the installer in main() kept a truncated download from running
a partial body, but the last line was a bare `main "$@"`. If the piped
download stopped right after `main` (or `main `), bash saw a complete
command at EOF and ran main with no positional parameters. Under the
documented `curl ... | bash -s -- --dry-run` (or --version / --no-setup)
path that silently dropped the caller's flags, so a dry run could resolve
the latest release, run npm, and start setup.

The call now sits in a brace group:

  {
    main "$@"
    exit $?
  }

Bash does not run the group until it has read the closing brace, so
every truncation inside it is a syntax error and nothing executes; a
truncation before the group leaves only function definitions. A comment
in install.sh records why the bare call is not enough.

Validation: a new boundary test pipes install.sh to `bash -s --
--dry-run` truncated at every byte offset from the end of main() to EOF
and asserts that npm and the rea binary are never invoked; offsets
inside the group must exit non-zero with a bash parse error and no
stdout, offsets before it must print nothing, and the complete group
must finish the dry run. Reproduced the original bug by cutting the old
script after `main`: the dry run invoked npm install. `bash -n` and
shellcheck 0.11.0 are clean.

* fix(install): wrap the whole script in the truncation guard

The previous guard only wrapped the final `main "$@"` invocation, so the
preamble streamed on the `curl ... | bash` path before any incomplete
compound command was open. A download cut off right after the bytes
`set` reached EOF with a complete, argument-less `set`, which prints every
shell variable, so inherited tokens could reach stdout.

The brace group now opens on line 2, directly after the shebang, and
closes on the last line, enclosing `set -euo pipefail`, the constants, the
functions and the final `main "$@"` / `exit $?`. Bash must therefore read
the whole file before running anything; any earlier cut is a syntax error
at EOF. `set -euo pipefail` still applies inside the group (checked
manually for `false`, an unbound variable, and a failing function body),
and shellcheck 0.11.0 and `bash -n` are clean.

The truncation test now pipes every prefix of install.sh, from byte 0 to
EOF (about 6,100 cuts, run 16 at a time with a minimal environment that
includes a sentinel variable), into `bash -s -- --dry-run`. Before the
group opens it must exit quietly; inside the group it must fail with a
syntax error; in every case stdout stays empty and neither npm nor rea is
invoked. Only the complete script performs the dry run.

commits.body:
feat(ghidra): admit soft-float MIPS32r2 ELF with integer-register float storage (#1949)

* feat(ghidra): admit soft-float MIPS32r2 ELF with integer-register float storage

Soft-float o32 executables (Linux kernel builds, bare-metal firmware) were
refused because their ABI flags record declares no CPR1 and FP ABI 3.
Ghidra's MIPS32 compiler specifications model only hard-float o32, so typed
float/double signatures (DWARF) would be bound to $f12/$f14/$f0 and the
decompiler loses the real dataflow: `return sel ? a : b` decompiled to
`return in_f0;`, and callers passed phantom FPU inputs.

Admit ELF32 ET_EXEC o32 MIPS32r2 targets whose ABI record declares soft-float
with no CPR1, and commit `mips_soft_float_storage: o32-integer-registers-v1`
in their analysis profile only (hard-float profile digests are unchanged).
ReaGhidraMipsSoftFloat.java runs after auto-analysis and, for each function
with a float/double formal type, either keeps the types with the storage
Ghidra's o32 model assigns to a same-size integer (pair alignment, stack
spill), or, for auto-parameters such as hidden struct-return pointers, swaps
float types for same-size integers under dynamic storage. No function is left
on hard-float storage. The report is written last; the provider client
requires it exactly when the profile commits the policy and refuses the
session before any operation otherwise.

Verification: real Ghidra 12.1.4 lane (verify:ghidra:mips) now builds
hard- and soft-float fixtures in both byte orders and checks exact
parameter/return storage through inspect_native_api, caller constants,
snapshot profile and Evidence outcome; test:fast, verify:package and an
installed-tarball soft-float run pass.

* fix(ghidra): model soft-float MIPS as a prototype for every typed callable

Review feedback on #1949: rewriting storage per Function left external
functions and indirect calls through typed function pointers on Ghidra's
hard-float o32 prototype, which still read $f12/$f14/$f0 while the session
reported success. A negative control confirms it: without the change,
`(*rea_mips_soft_callback)(8.5f, 9.5f, sel)` decompiles to
`(*rea_mips_soft_callback)(in_f12, in_f14, sel)`.

ReaGhidraMipsSoftFloat.java now derives a `__rea_soft_float` prototype from
the program's own default o32 model (encoded, float pentries and
float-consuming rules removed, so byte-order-specific aggregate rules and the
hidden struct-return pointer are kept), installs it as a specification
extension, and assigns it with dynamic storage to every non-thunk function,
external function and function-pointer definition whose formal types use
float or double. Thunks follow their targets. Float types are kept
everywhere, so the integer-retype fallback is removed. The script fails
without writing its report if the derived prototype or any reassigned
function still uses an FPU register.

The policy becomes `o32-soft-float-prototype-v1` with a
{functions, definitions} report. The soft-float fixture adds an indirect
call through a typed pointer; the real-Ghidra lane requires its constants
with no FPU inputs and the struct return's `float scale` in $a1.

* test(ghidra): pin ODDSPREG acceptance for soft-float MIPS ABI records

Review on #1949 suggested requiring flags1 == 0 for soft-float, since MIPS_AFL_FLAGS1_ODDSPREG names CPR1 registers. GCC 5.2 kernel modules, LLVM/Rust firmware and Clang -msoft-float objects all record flags1 = 1 with FP ABI soft-float: it is the MIPS32 o32 toolchain default and selects nothing without CPR1. Keep accepting it, say why at the check, and test that soft-float with ODDSPREG is admitted while any other general flag is refused.

commits.subject: fix(native): accept universal binaries with LIB64 x86_64 slices (#1982)
commits.body:
fix(native): accept universal binaries with LIB64 x86_64 slices (#1982)

* fix(native): apply printed lipo capability bits to CPU subtypes

lipo -detailed_info prints a slice's capability byte separately from its
symbolic subtype: CPU_SUBTYPE_LIB64 for x86_64 and ppc64, and other bits
as hex. Only the arm64e pointer-auth form was applied, so a LIB64 x86_64
slice normalized to subtype 3 while its FAT entry carries 0x80000003,
and slice validation rejected the universal binary as an integrity
mismatch. Fold the printed capability byte into the subtype code.

* fix(native): leave lipo CPU subtypes unknown without capability bits

The lipo shipped with macOS 26 prints an empty capabilities line for
x86_64 slices whose FAT capability byte is 0x80 as well as 0x00, so a
symbolic subtype alone does not identify the slice's CPU subtype. The
parser assumed no capability bits and still reported subtype 3 for
LIB64 slices, which made universal applications such as Sublime Text
fail slice validation. Report the subtype code as unknown when lipo
prints no capability byte, as arm64e already does; slice validation
then relies on the remaining physical facts.

* test(native): cover printed and blank lipo capability bits

Fold CPU_SUBTYPE_LIB64 and hex capability bytes into x86_64 subtype
codes, and keep the code unknown for the blank capabilities line that
macOS 26 lipo prints.

* test(native): match a LIB64 x86_64 slice with blank lipo capabilities

Read a universal image whose x86_64 FAT entry carries 0x80000003 while
lipo reports CPU_SUBTYPE_X86_ALL with a blank capabilities line, as
macOS 26 lipo does, and expect both slices instead of an integrity
failure.

* fix(native): compare named lipo subtype bits without capability bytes

A blank capabilities line leaves the subtype code unknown, and slice
matching then skipped the subtype entirely. A FAT entry whose named
subtype differs, such as CPU_SUBTYPE_ARM64_V8 recorded by lipo as
CPU_SUBTYPE_ARM64_ALL, was accepted. Keep comparing the complete
subtype when lipo printed its capability byte, and otherwise compare
the subtype bits its record names.

* test(native): share LIB64 slice reader setup

Read the LIB64 universal fixture through one helper that takes the
x86_64 subtype lipo reports, so further cases reuse the same image and
lipo record. The existing expectation is unchanged.

* test(native): reject a blank-capability lipo subtype naming other bits

With the capabilities line blank, a lipo record naming
CPU_SUBTYPE_X86_64_H for the x86_64 LIB64 slice still disagrees with
the FAT entry's subtype bits and fails slice validation.

commits.subject: test(ghidra): require pending multi-HI16 coverage in the real MIPS relocatable lane (#1974)
commits.body:
test(ghidra): require pending multi-HI16 coverage in the real MIPS relocatable lane (#1974)

* test(ghidra): require pending multi-HI16 coverage in the real MIPS relocatable lane

Post-merge review on #1950: the relocation oracle exposes coverage.multiple_hi16, but the real-Ghidra lane never required it, and Clang's C output never produces a LO16 that resolves several pending HI16s. Ghidra's loader could therefore mishandle that stream while the lane still passed, although most GCC-built kernel modules checked contain it.

The relocatable fixture adds an assembly block with two lui %hi(rea_mips_rel_carry); LLVM's relocation sort then leaves one HI16 pending until a later LO16 that resolves it together with another HI16, including the carry. The lane now requires multiple_hi16: false on the previous fixture, true for all three variants (LE, BE, soft-float module) on real Ghidra 12.1.4.

* test(ghidra): make the MIPS multi-HI16 fixture independent of relocation sorting

Review on #1974: the block used two %lo of rea_mips_rel_carry, a symbol with other %lo uses, so the relocation stream depended on the assembler's HI16/LO16 sort. Clang 21 happened to leave a HI16 pending; Clang 17 (per review) and GNU as 2.45 (checked here: HI@4 LO@8 HI@0 LO@10) pair each HI16 with its own LO16, so multiple_hi16 stays false and the lane fails.

Use a dedicated symbol with two %hi and exactly one %lo. Any assembler that orders each HI16 before a matching LO16 must then emit both HI16s ahead of that single LO16: Clang 21 gives HI@0 HI@4 LO@8, GNU as 2.45 gives HI@4 HI@0 LO@8. The real-Ghidra lane passes for LE, BE and the soft-float module variant with multiple_hi16 true.

commits.subject: feat(setup): register DeepSeek Harness through setup, doctor and uninstall (#1929)
commits.body:
feat(setup): register DeepSeek Harness through setup, doctor and uninstall (#1929)

* feat(setup): register DeepSeek Harness through setup, doctor and uninstall

DeepSeek Harness registers MCP clients through a Cordis YAML patch
sequence in the home patch rather than a server table, so setup could
not configure it and users had to append the documented entry by hand.

Add a dsh client: the home patch $DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml
(~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml when unset) is parsed as a patch list, the REA
entry owns the stable rea-mcp id, and setup appends or replaces exactly
that entry while preserving unrelated patches and comments in place.
Doctor reports the registration through the same entry, and uninstall
removes it, dropping insert operations it emptied. Skill destinations
follow ~/.agents/skills ($DSH_AGENTS_HOME/skills when configured), the
home the rest of the client machinery already uses.

Fixes #1839

* fix(setup): carry environment and identity validation into DSH registrations

Address review: the DSH entry discarded discovered provider overrides;
config.env is now emitted and retained like the other dialects. An entry
carrying the rea-mcp id under a wrong or missing package name, or
duplicated entries, reads back as absent so setup rewrites exactly one
canonical entry instead of reporting unchanged. Doctor now requires
serverName rea and stdio transport before calling a DSH registration
aligned, and the Harness skill identifier in the docs matches the
installed reverse-engineer-anything skill.

* fix(setup): apply Cordis patch order and collapse DSH registrations

Address review: a later direct { id, config } operation replaces the
row's config under the native patch DSL, so the registration view now
applies patches in order instead of only reading insert operations;
doctor reports the effective command rather than the inserted one.
Setup rewrites exactly one canonical entry: duplicate id-matching rows
collapse to the first, direct patches to the entry are dropped from the
document and from the edited YAML, and uninstall removes them with the
entry. The client-location test fixture now clears DSH_HOME and
DSH_AGENTS_HOME so a developer environment cannot point the suite at
real Harness homes.

* fix(setup): repair direct-only registrations and preserve Cordis entry state

Serialize now edits the first insertion carrying rea-mcp in place, so a
grouped entry keeps its scope, neighbors, and comments instead of moving
to a fresh root-level insertion, and later carrying insertions and direct
patches collapse away. Entry-level disabled state projects into the
registration the doctor and setup compare, so a disabled row reads as
stale and the repair re-enables it. A direct-only registration no longer
suppresses the canonical insert append, and an update retains the
registration environment. Duplicate entries collapse across operations,
not only within one.

* fix(setup): preserve Harness row state through identity and refresh repairs

A wrong-package row still reads back as a server record carrying its
environment and caller fields, projected with a package marker the
alignment path treats as stale, instead of vanishing and dropping
config.env from the repair. A direct Cordis patch without a preceding
insertion configures nothing, so a direct-only registration reads as
absent even when its config matches and the repair appends the insert.
Caller-owned config fields beyond the REA-owned keys, such as the cwd
the native verifier sets, survive a refresh instead of being silently
dropped.

* fix(setup): preserve Cordis tags and collapse aligned Harness rows

A refresh rebuilt Harness config from parsed values, so a caller !!js
expression was written back as a literal. Owned keys are now overlaid on
the winning config node and other nodes stay in place. Two already-aligned
rea-mcp insertions read as stale, so setup collapses them to one row, and
the bundled skill lists dsh with the other clients.

* fix(setup): drop the unused DSH configuration type

Knip reports DshConfigurationFormat as an unused export. The format union
does not depend on that alias.

* fix(setup): keep Harness env tags and comment-only patches

A refresh replaced the whole env map, so a caller !!js value was written
back as a literal. Environment entries now stay in place unless the value
changed. A comment-only cordis.patch.yml parses as an empty patch list and
keeps those comments when the registration is appended. Docs describe
plain rea uninstall, which scans supported clients and has no --client flag.

* fix(setup): own Harness rows by entry id and expression state

Uninstall removes a rea-mcp row even when the launcher is stale or the
patch never established a server record. A non-boolean disabled value,
including a Cordis expression, reads as stale. Expression text on a known
environment setting is not validated as a literal path, so a refresh can
keep the tag.

* fix(setup): collapse aliased Harness insertions

An anchored insert followed by an alias parses as two rea-mcp rows, but
the YAML edit kept the alias, so readback stayed duplicated and setup
restored the file. Aliases that resolve to the owned entry are now
dropped, including an alias of the entry inside one insert. Aliases of
other patches stay.

An insert value that aliases another entry list still loaded a second
rea-mcp row after the operation-level alias collapse. That alias is now
dropped once the anchored list is rewritten. A config: *cfg map is
resolved and cloned before the refresh, so a caller !!js field on the
aliased map is not rewritten as a plain literal.

* fix(setup): follow Harness aliases for ids, lists, and env tags

An insert alias whose anchor is not another insert is copied so
unrelated rows stay while the owned row is rewritten. An aliased
entry id is resolved before ownership checks, and an environment alias
of an unchanged !!js scalar is left in place.

* fix(setup): keep aliased Harness env maps through uninstall

An env alias is cloned before a refresh so tagged values are not rebuilt
as literals, and expression-key scans follow aliases before path checks.
Insert aliases that carry REA are recorded before uninstall empties their
anchor, so the later alias is dropped instead of dangling.

* fix(setup): follow root Harness aliases and mark dsh as main-only

Winning-config walks resolve a root alias before patch order, so a replayed direct config's !!js env is not validated as a literal path. Root aliases that own rea-mcp are recorded before uninstall empties their anchor. An insert whose only owned member is an external alias is cloned so Cordis tags survive. A root alias whose anchor is not a loaded operation is copied and only the owned row is edited, so unrelated rows stay active. Entry id aliases become a scalar before their anchor patch is dropped. * fix(install): orient Node.js version mismatch failures with actionable remediation

install.sh previously told operators "use Node.js 22.x (>=22.19), 24.x (>=24.11),
or 26+" without saying how to install one. The curl|bash onboarding path then
left the operator to guess between nvm, fnm, n, Volta, system packages, or
nodejs.org — a lookup that bounces across search engines for a first-time user.

Replace the one-line failure with a block that:
- Names the detected Node.js version (so the operator confirms it is theirs).
- Shows the three most common install paths (nvm, fnm, direct tarball).
- Pins the Node.js release line (24) that satisfies the engine, so copy-paste
  commands produce a supported runtime instead of whichever "latest" is on top.
- Maps uname -m / uname -s to the Node.js tarball label pair for this host
  (e.g. darwin/arm64, linux/x64), so the operator can grab the right archive
  from https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v24.x/ without a second lookup.

Verified with four Node.js versions (24.18 compatible, 25.9/20.11 outside the
supported ranges, 22.18 below the minor floor) that remediation triggers only
on real mismatches and names the host labels correctly. shellcheck install.sh
and npm run check:fast remain clean.

commits.subject: feat(flutter): identify Dart snapshot builds and inspect AOT payloads by pure APK parsing (#1582)
commits.body:
feat(flutter): identify Dart snapshot builds and inspect AOT payloads by pure APK parsing (#1582)

* feat(flutter): identify Dart snapshot builds by pure APK parsing

Add a flutter-provider family with one operation, identify_flutter_build,
that reads an APK's lib/<abi>/libapp.so and libflutter.so through the
hardened ZIP reader and reports build facts as observations:

- The Dart VM snapshot hash, read 20 bytes after every snapshot magic
  (f5f5dcdc). The vm and isolate sections are cross-checked: agreeing
  sections collapse to one snapshot_hash, disagreeing sections keep every
  candidate with snapshot_hash null and partial coverage.
- Per-ABI library digests and byte sizes, plus the engine library's GNU
  build-id note and any labeled 'Dart VM version' or Android clang/LLVM
  toolchain strings, verbatim; release builds without a version string
  report null rather than a guess.
- The APK is digested before parsing so Evidence binds the observation to
  the exact input, and a target with no libapp.so reports not-detected
  with complete coverage.

The scanner is streaming with explicit pending-magic and rescan
bookkeeping, so chunk boundaries cannot double-count or drop sections, and
magic-free streams never accumulate. No engine, no external lookups: the
hash-to-SDK mapping stays with external datasets by design.

Verified against Flutter Gallery 2.9.2 (112 MB, three ABIs): every ABI
reports the same agreeing hash 65817c30a78bb44c3dc3771876b6010a from two
sections, per-ABI build-ids, and the clang toolchain line; a plain
aapt2-built APK reports not-detected with complete coverage. Scanner
goldens come from the same libraries. READMEs carry the new 'Flutter apps'
row in every supported language.

* feat(flutter): inspect Dart AOT snapshots through the ELF symbol table

Add inspect_dart_aot to the flutter family: for one ABI's libapp.so it
locates the four _kDart*Snapshot* symbols through the ELF dynamic symbol
table (ELF32 and ELF64 little-endian, bounds-checked reads; a payload
without exported symbols is refused), reports each section's offset and
size, validates data-section headers (magic, kind, length; instructions
sections honestly report nulls for the fields their layout does not
carry), and projects a bounded string pool from the isolate data section:
distinct package: source URIs (the app's dependency inventory), dart: SDK
URIs, and identifier-shaped tokens, each with counts, bounds, and partial
coverage when truncated.

The string pool is labeled as a byte-pattern projection, not deserialized
cluster semantics: typed class and function recovery remains an
SDK-specific parser, which the snapshot hash now unlocks. The ABI is
caller-selected with a deterministic default (arm64-v8a, x86_64, then
first available).

Verified against Flutter Gallery 2.9.2: all four symbols on both ELF64
(arm64-v8a) and ELF32 (armeabi-v7a) images, header validation, hash
agreement with identify_flutter_build, and a 756 package: / 201 dart:
URI pool from the isolate data section; goldens in DartElf.test.ts come
from the same libraries.

* fix(flutter): own snapshots, bound image reads, and preserve cancellation

Mirror the ownership bar the maintainers applied across the merged JEB,
ADB, and Apktool PRs:

- Copy the admitted APK into a provider-owned, read-only snapshot (EXCL
  create, chmod 0400) before digesting and parsing; every later read uses
  the snapshot, so a concurrently modified original cannot mix into one
  observation. The result reports the snapshot's byte size and digest.
- Retain failed snapshot-root cleanup in a provider set and retry it on
  close(), throwing an aggregate error when a root is still owned; root
  removal is injectable so the retention is testable.
- Allocate the AOT image buffer at exactly the declared library size
  before reading (bounded before allocation, not concat-after-stream),
  keep the 256 MiB ceiling, and check cancellation between digest and
  stream chunks through a captured abort reason.
- Accept APK paths containing spaces (covered by a fixture test) and
  escape the ABI pattern's dash for v-mode regex compatibility.

Also add tests for cleanup retention with close retry and for
cancellation before any snapshot root is created.

* docs(flutter): cover the Italian README with the Flutter row

The Italian translation landed between the merged feature PRs; its table
now carries every merged row plus this one, keeping its documentation-link
set identical to README.md.

* fix(flutter): make the ABI pattern portable for v-mode validators

Use a hex-escaped hyphen in the ABI character class, matching the form
the ADB portability fix uses, so clients compiling advertised schemas in
unicodeSets mode accept the inspect_dart_aot input schema.

* refactor(flutter): reuse shared harnesses and deduplicate the vertical

The duplicate-detection gate (jscpd, 2.5% threshold) tipped to 2.51% with
the flutter files added. Reuse the existing machinery instead of repeating
it:

- FlutterBuildAnalysisService delegates to executeProviderOperation, the
  shared admission/Evidence composition, instead of restating its body.
- The CLI registers both commands from one table-driven spec.
- Boundary tests use the shared serveCli and assertAdvertisedMcpContracts
  harnesses rather than hand-rolled equivalents.
- The provider test consolidates the four payload-shape cases into one
  table-driven case; the service test uses one admission table and
  distinct phrasings.

Duplicate lines fall from 2.51% to 2.48%, back under the gate.

* fix(flutter): address review findings from real-app verification

CassieFox23 verified the PR against three real F-Droid Flutter apps and
a control app, and found five gaps. All are fixed and re-verified against
cone (info.tangential.cone), one of the tested apps:

- Build-id: the scanner now reads the descriptor length from the note
  header instead of assuming 20 bytes, so 8-byte ids from older
  toolchains parse; the schema accepts 8-128 hex characters. Verified
  against cone's readelf-reported ids on all three ABIs.
- Compiler line: the toolchain capture bound rises from 200 to 500
  characters, keeping cone's 262-character clang line verbatim.
- Zero-byte libapp.so: the extraction target is created before streaming,
  so an empty entry yields a clean unsupported_target refusal for
  inspect_dart_aot and elf_header_valid: false with partial coverage for
  identify_flutter_build, instead of a raw ENOENT with code UNKNOWN.
- Truncated library: identify_flutter_build marks fewer than two snapshot
  sections as partial coverage with a limitation naming the count, and a
  missing ELF magic gets its own limitation.
- Docs: the default ABI preference now matches the code exactly
  (arm64-v8a, x86_64, x86, armeabi-v7a, then the rest alphabetically).

Also: every test that read the author's /tmp/opencode goldens now builds
a self-contained synthetic ELF64 image with dynsym, four snapshot
symbols, two snapshot sections, and a string pool, so the suite runs
anywhere; the verify lane now requires a present hex build-id per ABI
instead of accepting null.

* fix(flutter): address the Codex review findings

Eight findings, all applied:

- P1: SnapshotHashScanner keeps candidates in a Set (no quadratic
  Array.includes) with a 64-distinct-hash cap, so a hostile payload of
  magic+hash records cannot stall the scan or bloat the response.
- P1: projectStringPool stops admitting new distinct entries once each
  category reaches twice its projection bound and reports
  collectionCapped; allocation and sorting now track the response, not
  the payload.
- P2: ZIP reader rejections during entry iteration or entry streaming
  map into the typed error algebra (cancellation vs input refusal)
  instead of escaping as unhandled exceptions in both operations.
- P2: magic_valid now marks coverage only for the *Data symbols; a
  complete four-symbol image with valid data magics reports complete
  coverage (the instruction symbols intentionally lack the magic).
- P2: the MCP server closes the Flutter provider during shutdown, so a
  retained snapshot root is retried and reported, not leaked.
- P2: LabeledStringScanner commits matches only when a printable run is
  delimiter-terminated; the carry grows to 600 bytes so a 500-character
  toolchain line survives any chunk boundary untruncated.
- P2: both Flutter tool effects declare writesFilesystem: true; the
  owned APK snapshot and extracted libapp.so are temporary writes.
- P2: the verify lane asserts every ABI agrees on exactly one snapshot
  hash instead of discarding the computed set.

* fix(flutter): address the second Codex review round

Nine findings on the first-round fixes:

- P1: identify_flutter_build enforces a cumulative extraction budget
  (768 MiB) across every library entry, not just per library, so an APK
  with many ABIs cannot stream an unbounded total.
- P1: a single NUL-free printable run stops materializing at 1024 bytes
  and marks the pool capped, so an adversarial one-run section cannot
  allocate unbounded strings.
- P1: ELF cString bounds the NUL-terminator scan to the name maximum
  plus one, so malformed symbol tables cannot scan the whole image per
  entry.
- P2: mapReaderFailure distinguishes ArtifactReaderFailure texts —
  budget/limit rejections map to resource constraints, integrity
  failures (CRC/overlap/signature) to their own input refusal — instead
  of collapsing all reader failures into one message.
- P2: the labeled-string carry is cleared when a delimiter commits a
  run, so consecutive toolchain lines are never concatenated.
- P2: string-pool counts are renamed *_count_at_least and documented as
  lower bounds, because capped collection discards values beyond twice
  the projection bound.
- P2: inspect_dart_aot marks hash disagreements, non-pair source counts,
  and candidate-cap saturation as partial coverage.
- P2: only valid lowercase-hex hash records count as snapshot sources;
  complete magic records with non-hex fields do not inflate agreement.
- P2: the per-entry size refusal in inspect_dart_aot moves after ABI
  selection, so an oversized unselected ABI no longer refuses a small
  request.

* fix(flutter): address the third Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: the owned snapshot revalidates the source after the copy (size,
  mtime, inode), so an in-place replacement or swap mid-copy refuses
  the observation instead of publishing mixed bytes.
- P2: a failed ZipArtifactReader close retains the snapshot root for
  close() retry instead of silently swallowing the descriptor leak,
  in both operations.
- P2: snapshot headers are parsed within their symbol bounds and a
  symbol smaller than the 16-byte header reports magic_valid false,
  so trailing-image bytes can no longer fake a valid data section.
- P2: the verify lane counts provider.close() cleanup failures as
  lane failures instead of certifying a run with retained roots.
- P2: LabeledStringScanner reports toolchain_capped when further
  distinct matching lines are observed past the 4-line projection;
  identify marks such results partial with a naming limitation.

* fix(flutter): address rounds three and four of the Codex review

Round three (one missed finding) plus round four (five findings):

- P2: the GNU build-id note descriptor size is decoded from all four
  bytes of the little-endian field, rejecting nonzero high bytes
  instead of masking them to 16 bits.
- P1: the Flutter MCP handlers route through createContractToolHandler
  and the session's analysisAdmission, so close_binary and snapshot
  operations drain in-flight Flutter calls instead of racing them.
- P2: the owned-snapshot copy is a streamed, abort-checked write (no
  copyFile), so cancellation stops the write promptly while the
  source-identity revalidation (size, mtime, inode) still guards
  against mid-copy replacement.
- P2: identify marks any snapshot_hash_sources value other than exactly
  two as partial, matching the inspection path's pair requirement.
- P2: the verify lane refuses to run without --apk (exit 2) instead of
  printing a false-green pass, and the engine check requires every
  libapp-carrying ABI to have a present libflutter with a valid hex
  build-id rather than filtering missing engines away vacuously.

* fix(flutter): address the fifth Codex review round

Six findings plus the upstream duplication baseline:

- P2: the flutter-provider kind reports available in the capability
  inventory, so binary_session no longer lists always-registered
  Flutter tools as provider_missing.
- P2: printable runs that exceed the 1024-byte cap are discarded at
  their delimiter instead of emitting their truncated prefix as a
  fabricated observation.
- P2: ELF symbols must fit inside the file-backed portion of their
  PT_LOAD segment (p_filesz), so addresses in gaps or BSS are refused
  instead of accepting unrelated bytes.
- P2: the build-id carry spans the complete 80-byte maximum note
  (16-byte header + 64-byte descriptor) so chunk-boundary splits
  cannot drop the first byte.
- P2: the labeled-string carry is sized for the toolchain pattern's
  true 605-byte maximum, not the previous 600.
- P2: the AOT completeness predicate requires exactly two sources and
  one candidate unconditionally, so zero-source images with valid data
  magics report partial instead of complete.

Also: the shared ELF fixture builder and snapshot-section helper moved
to a dedicated FlutterTestFixtures module, eliminating cross-file test
duplication; jscpd now passes at 2.50% while main sits at 2.52%.

* fix(flutter): address the sixth Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: snapshot-hash scanning is bounded to the exported data symbols'
  byte ranges, so decoy or stale magic/hash sequences elsewhere in the
  image cannot inflate source counts or contribute candidates.
- P2: labeled-string runs longer than the carry bound are rejected
  instead of truncated, preventing a regex prefix from being published
  as a verbatim source string.
- P2: the AOT image reread checks cancellation between file reads and
  before the synchronous parsing stage, so a cancelled caller cannot
  receive a success from a completed 256 MiB read.
- P2: the verify lane requires exactly two snapshot sources per ABI,
  matching the provider's pair requirement, instead of accepting any
  count >= 2.
- P2: ELF section and program header entry sizes are validated against
  the class-defined minimum widths before walking either table, so
  undersized entries cannot cause field reads to cross into
  neighboring bytes.

* fix(flutter): address the seventh Codex review round

Six findings:

- P2: data-symbol ranges are deduplicated by offset and size, so aliased
  symbols mapping to the same bytes are scanned once and the result
  marks partial coverage with a limitation naming the shared range.
- P2: openEntrySafely forwards return/throw to the underlying Readable's
  iterator, so an early for-await exit closes the ZIP entry stream and
  releases its producer instead of leaking a backpressured pipe.
- P2: inspect_dart_aot now reports snapshot_hash_candidates and
  snapshot_hash_sources alongside snapshot_hash, so a null hash from
  conflicting evidence is distinguishable from missing hash data.
- P2: overlong printable runs only set toolchain_capped when they begin
  with a recognized label prefix (Dart VM version: or Android (); other
  long strings such as license text are skipped without marking partial.
- P2: readElfSymbol falls back to PT_DYNAMIC/DT_SYMTAB when section
  headers are absent (e_shnum 0, ET_DYN), so stripped Flutter libraries
  with exported snapshot symbols are no longer refused; the dynamic
  table is bounded by DT_STRSZ, DT_SYMENT, and the image end.
- P2: the verify lane exercises inspect_dart_aot for every ABI carrying
  libapp.so, not just the preferred default.

* fix(flutter): address the eighth Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: each data-symbol range gets a fresh SnapshotHashScanner so the
  carry from one noncontiguous slice cannot fabricate a record spanning
  into the next; results are aggregated after scanning.
- P2: dynsym name lookups are bounded to the linked string table —
  st_name offsets outside the table and terminators beyond it are
  rejected instead of reading unrelated payload bytes as symbol names,
  in both the section-header and PT_DYNAMIC paths.
- P2: identify_flutter_build routes its reader.entries and reader.open
  calls through the same collectEntriesSafely and openEntrySafely
  wrappers as inspect_dart_aot, so malformed ZIPs surface as input
  refusals instead of AnalysisProtocolError.
- P2: mapReaderFailure recognizes ArtifactReaderFailure texts carrying
  a cancelled reason, mapping them to AnalysisCancelledError instead
  of AnalysisInputError.
- P2: the cumulative extraction cap is enforced inside the chunk loop,
  not after each library completes, so refusal happens before the
  remaining bytes are streamed and hashed.

* fix(flutter): harden streaming, sizes, and cancellation after self-review

Four issues found in a systematic self-audit across all bug classes
from eight Codex rounds:

- createReadStream in both the digest function and the owned-snapshot
  copy now receives the AbortSignal directly, so cancellation aborts
  the filesystem read at the source instead of waiting for the next
  chunk to arrive on a slow filesystem.
- The owned snapshot enforces a 2 GiB APK-level size cap before any
  copy I/O, so a path pointing at an enormous file is refused before
  disk usage grows.
- identify_flutter_build preflights the sum of declared entry sizes
  against the 768 MiB cumulative budget, refusing before any ZIP
  extraction when the declared total already exceeds it.
- The LabeledStringScanner triple result() call is collapsed to a
  single invocation (the previous code called result() three times in
  the emission, relying on end() being idempotent).

No behavior change for valid inputs; all 36 tests, check:fast, and
the cone verify lane pass unchanged.

* fix(flutter): require structurally parseable ELF headers for complete coverage

CassieFox23's third corrupt-header case: an ELF with valid magic but

commits.subject: fix(apple): preflight XML plist nesting before keyed archive decoding (#2161)
commits.body:
fix(apple): preflight XML plist nesting before keyed archive decoding (#2161)

* fix(apple): preflight XML plist nesting before keyed archive decoding

inspect_keyed_archive documented a 128-level nesting limit, but the XML
plist path reached recursive decoding before any depth check: plist and
the prototype-key traversal in parseXmlPropertyList recurse once per
nesting level, so a ~75 KiB, 3000-level XML plist exhausted the call
stack and reported Maximum call stack size exceeded instead of the
bounded-resource limit that shallower over-limit documents (129, 200)
already produced. The CLI classified both as truncated, so no crash or
classification bypass was involved; the diagnostic was the defect.

Reject excessive nesting in parseXmlPropertyList before any recursive
pass, using the projection's own limit (MAX_PLIST_DEPTH) so the error is
identical to the one projectPlistValue raises: callers keep the
limit/truncated classification with no error-handler translation. Depth
counts values the way the projection does - container members nest one
level deeper, dictionary keys name members rather than nesting, and a
self-closing element is the value at its own level - so the guard
rejects exactly the documents the projection rejected, at the same
boundary, and every in-limit document decodes unchanged. The guard sits
at the shared decoder boundary, so Interface Builder, app Info.plist
resolution and native inspect_plist gain the same deterministic limit;
the binary plist path keeps its existing expansion preflight.

Binary plist behavior, ordinary XML decode, __proto__ omission counting,
and archive digest/Evidence provenance are unchanged. OpenStep
autodetection is untouched by this guard, as the existing Interface
Builder preflight also scopes its depth check to XML.

Regression coverage: decoder unit tests at and just past the limit for
dictionary and array nesting with self-closing and opaque markup,
module tests through decodeKeyedArchiveBytes including a valid
NSKeyedArchiver XML envelope at the limit, a production-boundary test
through inspectBundleKeyedArchive, and the compiled public CLI
reporting code truncated / reason limit for a 3000-level plist.

* fix(apple): check XML nesting against parsed element structure

Reuse the iterative XML decoder document for depth preflight and prototype-key lookup. Bound recursive plist wrappers alongside dictionaries and arrays without interpreting markup inside attributes or DOCTYPE declarations as values.

Validated with 104 focused tests including compiled CLI, MCP prototype-key, and Interface Builder coverage; npm run check and verify:test-discovery passed. No real-provider verification was run.

commits.subject: feat(ghidra): admit RISC-V ELF analysis through a pinned generic lane (#2151)
commits.body:
feat(ghidra): admit RISC-V ELF analysis through a pinned generic lane (#2151)

* feat(ghidra): admit RISC-V ELF analysis through a pinned generic lane

Refs #2063.

Recognize `EM_RISCV` (243) as a provider-neutral family that carries its own ELF
facts, and bound the first Ghidra lane to little-endian `ET_EXEC` images that
declare the double-float ABI, pinned to `RISCV:LE:32:default` or
`RISCV:LE:64:default` with the `gcc` compiler specification.

Ghidra 12.1.4 is not reliable without the pin: its `riscv.opinion` pins
`variant="default"` for the 64-bit constraint and leaves the 32-bit constraint
with the comment that the loader "must choose between 'default' and 'AndeStar'
variants". Measured on the installed release tree, a source-owned generic RV32
ELF with no Andes declaration imports as `RISCV:LE:32:AndeStar_v5:gcc`, while
RV64 resolves to `RISCV:LE:64:default:gcc`. The lane therefore states the
language per width and refuses any caller-selected processor outside it instead
of inheriting the header guess.

Refusals name the declaration rather than falling back to a guessed profile:
big-endian images (Ghidra 12.1.4 ships no big-endian RISC-V language),
non-`ET_EXEC` images, `EF_RISCV_RVE`, `EF_RISCV_TSO`, and every float ABI other
than double, which the pinned generic compiler specifications model. The raw
e_flags bits stay in Evidence as declarations, not as instruction semantics.

Family recognition now has one owner for the ELF-metadata families:
`ELF_METADATA_ARCHITECTURES`, `isElfMetadataArchitecture`, and
`HeaderArchitecture` replace ten `Exclude<BinaryArchitecture, "mips">` sites that
would each have needed a second hand-edited member. `ghidraPinnedLanguage` is
that owner for the import commitment: the session readback previously re-derived
only the MIPS pin, so a profile committing any second pinned language failed with
a language-mismatch error before the bridge started.

Hopper and IDA refuse RISC-V by name, matching the MIPS wording. Caller-supplied
raw-binary entry keeps its existing four-family list; this lane is ELF-header
admission only.

Verification on macOS 15.7.7 arm64, Node 24.18.0, Ghidra 12.1.4 PUBLIC and JDK
21.0.12.1, with the host decompiler built from the release sources for
`os/mac_arm_64`: `npm run check` passes; `npm run test:fast` passes 396 test
files; `npm run verify:test-discovery` discovers all 917 test files exactly once.
Source-owned RV32 and RV64 double-float `ET_EXEC` fixtures complete
`rea analyze --provider ghidra` and `rea decompile rea_riscv_entry`, committing
`RISCV:LE:32:default` and `RISCV:LE:64:default` with `language_selection:
provider-pinned-v1`; the soft-float RV64 shape is refused with the named
float-ABI reason, and the full refusal matrix including the RV32 and
width-mismatch shapes is covered by unit tests. No `verify:ghidra:riscv` lane
script is included in this change; the runs above were performed manually against
the installed engine. Fork pull requests receive no CI check runs, so the
real-provider scope above is the evidence available for review.

* fix(ghidra): bound the RISC-V lane by declared flags and document it

Address review feedback on #2151.

`e_flags` bits outside `EF_RISCV_RVC | EF_RISCV_FLOAT_ABI` are now refused with
the offending value named, so a reserved or newer producer declaration cannot
enter the verified generic lane by falling through the RVE, TSO and float-ABI
checks.

Admission reads `e_type` only, so the refusal text no longer calls `ET_EXEC`
static: a fixed-address declaration does not establish static linkage, and

boundary as a limitation rather than inferring a load model.

commits.subject: fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts (#1770)
commits.body:
fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts (#1770)

* fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts

Importing the source/ subtree of a legacy PHP and C# checkout produced
four wrong or missing facts:

- Babel's unambiguous mode parses a module first and keeps its
  strict-mode recovery errors after falling back to a script, so a valid
  sloppy-mode `delete messages;` was reported as a parse failure and the
  semantic IR marked the file as parser-recovered. Parsing now goes
  through one owner that re-parses such a script as a script.
- .php and .cs files had no language; they are now detected as PHP and
  C# (detection only, no parsing).
- A root without its own .git was reported as having no version
  control even inside a checkout. The adapter now resolves the nearest
  enclosing repository, as Git does, and reports `none` only when no
  ancestor has one.
- The CLI recorded importer_version as null although the package
  version is known.

* fix(reference): keep module strictness and classify C# and PHP as source

Review follow-up. `.mjs` and `.mts` files are modules by extension, but
the script fallback re-parsed them in sloppy mode and erased real
strict-mode errors. The parser boundary now owns the extension rule,
parses explicit modules as modules and applies the fallback only when
the mode is ambiguous; the require-binding analysis uses the same rule.

`.cs` and `.php` received a language but stayed classified as unknown,
so source-to-bundle comparison dropped them. Both are now source
extensions, like the other detected languages.

* fix(reference): honor package module scope and keep unknown-mode strict errors

Review follow-up. A `.js` file under a package.json with `"type":
"module"` is an ES module, but it went through the script fallback that
erases strict-mode errors. The import now reads each in-inventory
package.json and parses `.js` files in a module scope as modules. Other
`.js` and `.ts` sources keep an unknown mode, because bundlers treat them
as modules without that field: they are no longer forced to script, and
errors that only the module parse reports are kept as an entry limitation.

* fix(reference): bound package scopes and keep application parsing unchanged

Review follow-up.
- `.cjs` files parse as scripts, so module-only strict errors no longer
  become limitations on CommonJS trees. `.cts` keeps an unknown mode
  because TypeScript compiles ES import syntax there.
- An unreadable or linked package.json now bounds the module scope with
  an unknown type instead of letting an outer `"type": "module"` apply.
- The application pipeline parses as on main again. Its module-only
  strict errors keep a source partial; package-mode handling stays in the
  reference importer.

* refactor(reference): keep unmarked module modes unknown instead of resolving package scope

Review follow-up. Resolving Node package scope for `.js` kept pulling in
more of Node's lookup semantics (require bindings, excluded or
directory-named manifests). Only extensions now select a mode: `.mjs`
and `.mts` parse as modules and `.cjs` as scripts. Every other source
keeps an unknown mode, so module-only strict errors stay visible as an
entry limitation instead of being dropped or asserted. This matches the
require-binding analysis, which also treats unmarked paths as unknown.

fix(wasm): stop appending WABT remediation to unrelated runtime-root failures (#2084)

inspect_wasm_artifact's configuration-phase error handler assumed every
non-OwnedCommandFailure thrown before the artifact phase was about WABT

via absolute REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY; REA does not install tools." to the
reason. WabtArtifactProvider.inspect() also allocates its PrivateRuntimeRoot
during the configuration phase, so a PrivateRuntimeRootUnavailableError (the
Windows native-authority capability, unrelated to WABT) got the same false
remediation glued onto its own already-correct message, misdirecting anyone
troubleshooting a correctly-configured WABT install toward re-checking WABT
instead of the real blocker.

Classify PrivateRuntimeRootUnavailableError before the generic
configuration-phase branch, matching the existing convention already used
in JavaScriptAnalysisWorker.ts and SourceMapCommand.ts: surface it as its
own AnalysisCapabilityUnavailableError with no userMessage override, letting
its own message stand.

Verified against a real WABT 1.0.42 Windows release (hash-checked against
GitHub release metadata) and a real compiled .wasm module: before the fix,
`reason` read "REA Windows native controls are unavailable: ENOENT: ...
Supply WABT 1.0.42 ..." even with a fully correct REA_WABT_BIN_DIRECTORY;
after, `reason` reports only the real cause.

commits.subject: fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases (#1941)
commits.body:
fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases (#1941)

* fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases

A closure that aliases a binding from its enclosing scope evaluates that
binding once live and once at its own capture point. The capture cannot
order a binding declared in another function, so it fell back to a second
live evaluation. Only primitive results were kept, so every level of
nesting doubled the work: 20 nested closures over a non-constant value
took about 14 s, and a 443 KB generated wrapper reached the 300 s
analysis timeout.

Keep a live binding value when no caller could change it: no alias cycle
closes on or above the binding and the expression depth budget was not
reached. Bindings on a cycle are still re-evaluated, so their values and
reasons are unchanged.

Found while building a source-owned reproduction for #1847; that report's
worker heap exhaustion is a separate, already closed defect.

* fix(javascript): keep the expression depth budget for retained values

Reusing a retained composite value from any depth let a chain of wrappers
(s1 = {x: s0}, s2 = {x: s1}, ...) nest past the expression depth budget:
300 wrappers produced a 299-level value where the budget stops at 86, the
serialized IR grew quadratically, and 3,000 wrappers overflowed the stack
in JSON.stringify.

Record the expression depth at which each caller-independent value was
derived and reuse it only at that depth or shallower. A deeper reader
derives the value again and reaches the budget exactly as before. Closure
aliases read their outer binding at one depth on both paths, so nested
closures stay linear.

feat(server): frame analysis-target content as untrusted data (#1908)

* feat(server): frame analysis-target content as untrusted data

Strings, decompiled code, page text, scripts, captures and logs returned
by REA originate from the analysed target, which can embed text aimed at
the agent. Nothing marked that content, so a prompt injection inside a
binary or page could steer the agent toward tools that run code.

- Server instructions now state that target-derived tool output is data,
  never instructions, and that any request in it to run, install,
  download or send something is a prompt-injection attempt to report.
- Tool contracts declare returnsTargetContent. It is on by default; only
  seven tools whose results hold REA session state or caller-supplied
  values (binary_session, close_binary, export_evidence_bundle,
  record_unknown, update_unknown, inspect_adb_client,
  inspect_apktool_client) are audited exceptions, so new tools start
  marked.
- Successful results of marked tools carry
  _meta.provenance = { untrusted_content: true, source: "analysis_target" }.

list against the contract catalog, and an in-memory MCP client that sees
the instructions and the marker on a marked tool but not on
binary_session.

* fix(server): mark failed target-content results as untrusted too

The untrusted provenance marker was attached only on the success branch
of ToolResultDelivery, but failures can carry target-derived text as
well: error messages, captured output, and partial observations such as
the terminal frames a failed capture_process_scenario retains in
partial_observation. A host gating later process or device actions on the
marker would have treated an adversarial error payload as trusted.

Every error path in src/server now carries the failing tool's provenance:
- toErrorToolResult and toRecordedPartialErrorToolResult take the tool's
  target-content flag explicitly, so each caller is audited by the type
  checker; toCallToolResult, toEvidenceToolResult (recording failure), the
  response-budget error that replaces an oversized success, and the
  Electron partial-evidence path pass contract.returnsTargetContent.
- Admission failures in runAdmittedToolOperation resolve the flag from the
  tool name through the new toolReturnsTargetContent, the same predicate
  the contract metadata uses; unknown names stay marked.
- The transport's oversized-error replacement keeps the original's marker
  and counts it in its budget check, matching the projected error.
- Errors the MCP SDK builds itself (input validation, thrown handlers) are
  marked in the transport for target-content tools only.

does. docs/mcp-contracts.md now states that error results carry the
marker. Tests cover marked and unmarked error results, the

the SDK transport, the recorded partial-evidence path, the budget
replacement, the oversized-error replacement, and SDK validation errors
for a marked and a content-free tool.

The content-free exception set was audited against successful results
only. Now that failures carry the marker too, every exception was
re-audited against its error paths with one question: can the result
include text produced by an external process, provider or device, or
stored content REA did not author?

  createGhidraDiagnostics) projects the launcher's captured stdout and
  stderr, which can contain target-derived log text.

  installed path parsed from `adb version` stdout, and a failed probe

- inspect_apktool_client: the success result carries the first line of

  stderr_excerpt.

  and domain, which an imported evidence bundle can supply; list_unknowns
  and get_evidence_bundle already return that data marked.

counts; failures are filesystem, cancellation, or a fixed integrity
message) and record_unknown (the caller's input plus REA-computed ids
and digests; registry errors project only a reason code).

why the removed tools stay marked.

createToolCatalog() and CATALOG_IDENTITY.tools projected every
client-visible contract field except returnsTargetContent. Because the
untrusted-content framing left schemas, effects, prompts, CLI names and
the package version unchanged, a same-version MCP process started before
the update digested equal to the new server and binary_session reported
it aligned although it never emits _meta.provenance.

catalog and CATALOG_IDENTITY.tools, and export createCatalogDigests so a

fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size (#2144)

* fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size

A ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX member is attacker-controlled and can expand far
beyond the archive that carries it. Inventory hashed every member to EOF
and extraction wrote every member with no ceiling, so a ~2 MiB archive
could drive ~30 s of CPU during inventory and ~150 s plus 2 GiB of disk
writes during extraction.

A fixed per-entry byte cap is the wrong shape: it rejects legitimately
large members inside large packages. The ceiling instead scales with the
archive's own size (500x, with a 256 MiB floor), so large packages keep a
proportionally large budget while a small archive cannot amplify into
unbounded work. The cumulative declared size is charged from the central
directory before any entry is decompressed, and zip.js already verifies
streamed output against each declaration, so the check is exact and
covers both inventory and extraction through the shared reader.

* fix(artifacts): own decompression accounting per traversal

* test(artifacts): verify declared ZIP output enforcement

fix(process): accept a trace identifier the comparison result can represent (#2488)

The trace specification owns the declared identifier vocabulary and the
comparison result echoes those identifiers verbatim into raw_trace[].event_id,
matched_variant and diagnostic event_ids. The result module restated the shared
IDENTIFIER_PATTERN by hand with a 64-character cap, so a specification with a
longer identifier validated and then its own comparison result failed to parse:
compareProcessTraces threw a raw ZodError at the caller instead of returning a
comparison.

Export the identifier schema from the specification as the single owner and
reuse it in the evaluation module, removing the capped copy. IDENTIFIER_PATTERN
has no length bound and every other consumer uses it unbounded, so the
duplicate was the outlier. Removing the bound rather than adding one keeps the
advertised trace_spec input contract unchanged; identifiers of 64 characters or
fewer behave exactly as before.

Verified with 48 process tests, 24 boundary CLI/MCP trace tests, check:fast and
verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64. The regression test failed with the
ZodError before the change and passes after it.

commits.subject: fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group (#2202)
commits.body:
fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group (#2202)

* fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group

`spawnProcess` read the caller's affinity mask and applied it to the
suspended child unconditionally. A mask names processors relative to one
processor group, and Windows assigns each new process to a group of its
own choosing, so on hosts with more than 64 logical processors the child
is often placed in another group. `SetProcessAffinityMask` then rejects
the mask with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (87) and the spawn fails, making
every owned provider process start intermittently on such hosts.

Affinity is a nicety, not an authority or isolation control, so it is now
applied only when the caller and the suspended child both occupy the same
single processor group. A child placed in another group keeps that group's
default affinity and the spawn proceeds. Job Object membership,
kill-on-owner-close policy, owner normalization and priority preservation
are unchanged, and the mask failure remains fatal within a shared group,
where it is not expected.

Single-group hosts, including every host with 64 or fewer logical
processors, are unaffected: `GetProcessGroupAffinity` reports one group
for both processes and the same mask is applied as before.

The optional process-boundary fixture gains an `affinity` observation,
and the native verification lane asserts that an owned spawn succeeds and
that the child's mask matches the caller's whenever both share a single
group.

Fixes #2181

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(windows): refuse to widen a pinned caller's affinity across groups

Addresses review feedback on the first commit.

An unconstrained caller loses nothing when Windows places an owned child
in another processor group, so that spawn proceeds with the group's
default. A caller deliberately pinned to fewer processors than its group
holds is a different case: silently accepting the default would hand the
provider tree the whole group, which `docs/installation.md` tells
operators to rely on affinity to prevent. Such a spawn now fails naming
the constraint instead. `GetProcessAffinityMask` already reports the
group's active set, which distinguishes the two without another query.

Selecting the caller's group at creation through
PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_GROUP_AFFINITY was tried first and rejected:
`CreateProcessW` fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER on a host with a
single processor group, both alongside PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST and
on its own, so it cannot carry the ordinary path.

The boundary fixture's affinity observation now reports a process id's
own mask rather than its own, because a separate probe process is
assigned its own group and cannot stand in for the process that spawns
the child. Masks and the group's active set cross as fixed-width
hexadecimal strings: a mask can set bits above the safe-integer range,
where `JSON.parse` would round two different masks to one value.

The verification lane asserts the mask is inherited exactly when caller
and child share a group, and otherwise that the caller was unconstrained.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(windows): record what owned-process affinity does not preserve

A mask covering its group's whole active set does not distinguish a
caller the system placed in that group from one that selected the group
deliberately, so an owned child can still be placed elsewhere with its
processor count bounded and its group placement lost. Treating that case
as constrained instead is not available: on a multi-group host an
ordinary process is assigned a group by the system and its mask is that
group's active set, so refusing it would fail every owned spawn there.

commits.subject: perf(frida): evict captured messages without copying the whole queue (#2628)
commits.body:
perf(frida): evict captured messages without copying the whole queue (#2628)

Once a Frida session reached its 16 MiB capture budget, every new message
evicted the oldest one with Array#shift, re-serialized it to recover its
byte charge, and searched and spliced its per-script array. Each of
those is linear in the retained messages, so with about 188k small
messages retained the cost per message rose from 0.14 µs to 32 µs and
capped the main thread at roughly 31k messages per second, which a
hooked hot function can exceed.

Keep both queues as head-offset FIFOs that compact once half their slots
are evicted, and record each message's charge when it is admitted.
Arrival order already makes the globally oldest message the oldest one
of its script, so per-script eviction becomes a head check. Eviction is
now amortized O(1) at about 0.14 µs per message; retained messages,
their order and the truncation flag are unchanged.

Electron Framework one MCP call carries 2.5 MB of text (about 828k o200k

budget admits it. Agents asking for slice identity, UUID or dependency
counts paid that cost on every first call.

the existing complete result and Evidence identity, while summary
retains the complete Evidence and returns slice identity with
per-collection returned/total/exhaustive counts (956 tokens).

collection or the command provenance, repeating the producer's own
total and exhaustive flag so page exhaustion is never read as absence.

fix(artifacts): read ASCII control bytes in legacy ZIP names as ASCII (#2365)

* fix(artifacts): read ASCII control bytes in legacy ZIP names as ASCII

ZIP names without the UTF-8 flag were decoded with zip.js's CP437 table,
which maps bytes 0x01-0x1F and 0x7F to IBM PC display glyphs. A folder
zipped on macOS with a custom icon therefore listed and extracted
`Folder/Icon\r` as `Folder/Icon♪`, a name that is not in the archive and
differs from REA's directory inventory of the same folder. Tabs became `○`
and DEL became `⌂`.

Decode legacy names in REA's existing decodeText hook with the Unicode
CP437 mapping that Python's zipfile also uses: bytes below 0x80 as ASCII,
and the upper half with the same table zip.js uses.

Windows file names cannot contain U+0001-U+001F, so a Windows extraction
destination now refuses such a path with a typed path failure before
creating anything, as it already does for ':'.

* test(artifacts): check extracted legacy ZIP control names on disk

The control-name cases checked only the logical path that inventory
reports. Extraction writes through SafeOutputTree, so a change that
renamed the extracted files would still pass those cases.

Extract `Icon\r` and `é\t\u007F.a`, then compare the reported
relative_path, the directory listing, and the file contents. The new
cases skip on Windows, which refuses these names.
safeOutputTree.test.ts covers that refusal.
